passages.happening:
When the whole nation is across, God gives Joshua one more instruction. Twelve men, one from each tribe, are to go back into the middle of the Jordan, to the place where the priests are standing. Each is to lift a stone onto his shoulder and carry it to the place where Israel will camp that night (verses 2-5).

Joshua tells them what the stones are for. They are ‘to serve as a sign among you’. “In the future, when your children ask, ‘What do these stones mean to you?’ you are to tell them, ‘The waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it crossed the Jordan, the waters were cut off.’ Therefore these stones will be a memorial to the Israelites forever” (verses 6-7).

The men do it. The chapter adds that Joshua also set up twelve stones in the riverbed itself, where the priests' feet had been. “And the stones are there to this day” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This chapter tells the crossing again from another side. Hebrew storytelling often does this. It gives the outline first and then goes back to fill in a part of it. A reader should not expect the verses to run in strict order of time.

Standing stones and heaps of stones were used all over the ancient world to mark graves, borders, treaties and holy events. Jacob set one up at Bethel. Moses set up twelve pillars at Sinai for the twelve tribes. Most people could not read. A stone that would stand for generations, with a story attached, was how a people kept its memory.

The number is the point. There is one stone for each tribe, and that includes the tribes whose homes were back on the east side of the river. The crossing belonged to the whole people.

The stones are meant to make children ask. Israel taught its faith at home in this way. At the Passover meal a child was expected to ask what the meal meant, and the parent answered with the story of the exodus. The stones at Gilgal work like that meal. Something is put where a child will notice it, and the adult must be ready with the story.

The answer the parents are given says nothing about Israel's courage or Joshua's leadership. It says that the waters were cut off before the ark. The memorial is about what God did.

The words ‘to this day’ are the voice of the writer, speaking some time later to readers who could go and look. They are one of the signs that the book was written, or finished, after the events it tells.
passages.later:
The Passover had been given the same shape: “When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’ you are to reply, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt’” (Exodus 12:26-27).

At a Passover meal Jesus gave his followers a sign to repeat and a story to tell with it: “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me” (Luke 22:19).
passages.asks: God assumed that children would ask, and told the parents to have an answer. Ask what in your home, your habits or your calendar would make a child ask what it means. And ask what your answer would be: a story about what you did, or about what God did. If no one in your life is asking, ask what you could set up where it will be seen.

passages.t: The priests stand until everyone is across
passages.happening:
The priests with the ark stay in the middle of the Jordan until everything God told Joshua has been done. “The people hurried across” (verse 10). When all have crossed, the priests cross too, in the sight of the people (verse 11).

The fighting men of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh go over at the front, armed, as they had promised. About 40,000 troops cross onto the plains of Jericho (verses 12-13).

“On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they revered him all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses” (verse 14).

Then God tells Joshua to call the priests up out of the river. As soon as their feet touch dry land, ‘the waters of the Jordan returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The ark is the center of every scene. The water is cut off in front of it. The priests stay with it in the riverbed while a whole people passes. And the river comes back only when the ark comes out. The writer wants no one to think the Jordan happened to run low that day.

The people hurry. That small detail is honest. They were walking between a river that had stopped and a river that might start again, and they did not linger.

The eastern tribes keep the promise of chapter 1. Their families are safe at home across the river. They go in first all the same.

The number 40,000 is one of several large numbers in these books. The Hebrew word for ‘thousand’ can also mean a clan or a unit of soldiers. Some scholars read numbers like this one in that way, and others take them as they stand.

God had said in chapter 3 that he would begin to make Joshua great in Israel's eyes. This verse says he did. Joshua's standing with the people comes from what God did in front of them. It is given to him, and the people's respect for him lasts his whole life.

The name ‘ark of the Testimony’ in verse 16 is another name for the ark of the covenant. The Testimony is the tablets of the law that lay inside it.
passages.later:
After the Red Sea the same thing was said of Moses: “the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses” (Exodus 14:31).

Israel later learned that the ark was not a charm that worked by itself. In the days of Eli the people carried it into battle to force a victory, and they were defeated and the ark was taken (1 Samuel 4). What mattered at the Jordan was the God whose presence the ark stood for.
passages.asks: The priests stood in the riverbed, holding the weight, until the last person was over. Ask who has stood like that for you, and whether you have thanked them. Then ask who is counting on you to stay where you are until they are across, and what makes you want to leave early.

passages.t: ‘What is the meaning of these stones?’
passages.happening:
The chapter gives the date. “On the tenth day of the first month the people went up from the Jordan and camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho” (verse 19). There Joshua sets up the twelve stones from the river (verse 20).

He tells Israel again what to say to their children. “In the future, when your children ask their fathers, ‘What is the meaning of these stones?’ you are to tell them, ‘Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground.’” (verses 21-22).

Then he ties this day to an older one. God dried up the Jordan ‘just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over’ (verse 23).

And he gives the purpose. “He did this so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, and so that you may always fear the LORD your God” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The date is not a passing detail. The first month is the month of the exodus. The tenth day was the day each household in Egypt had been told to choose its Passover lamb. Forty years later, to the day, Israel stands in the promised land. The Passover itself will be kept four days later, in the next chapter.

Gilgal lay between the river and Jericho. Its exact site has not been found. It became Israel's base camp for the first part of the book, and it stayed an important place for centuries. Samuel visited it on his rounds as a judge, and Saul was confirmed as king there.

Joshua speaks of the Red Sea as something God did ‘before us’. Most of the people listening had not been born then, or had been children. Israel spoke of its history this way. What God did for one generation he did for the whole people, and those who came later were taught to say ‘we’.

The last verse gives two purposes, and they point in two directions. The first looks outward. God acted so that ‘all the peoples of the earth’ would know his power. Even at the moment of Israel's entry into the land, the book says that God has the whole world in view. Rahab, in chapter 2, has already shown what it looks like when someone from another people hears and believes.

The second looks inward. Israel is to ‘fear the LORD’ always. In the Old Testament this fear is not terror of a tyrant. It is the reverence and awe that a person owes to God, and it shows itself in trust and obedience.
passages.later:
The psalms keep the two crossings together as one work of God: “He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot; there we rejoiced in Him” (Psalm 66:6).

The purpose in verse 24, that all peoples should know, is the direction in which the risen Jesus sends his followers: “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19).
passages.asks: Joshua said ‘before us’ about something most of his hearers had never seen. Ask which of God's acts, in the Bible or in the generations before you, you can call your own story. Then look at the two purposes in the last verse. Ask whether your faith faces only inward, toward your own life with God, or whether anyone outside has come to know something of God because of it.
